title: Number Play: Supercells, Palindromes and Number Puzzles
seo_title: Number Play Class 6 Worksheet with Answers (NCERT Chapter 3)
standard_text: Numbers in patterns and puzzles: supercells, palindromes, the Kaprekar constant 6174, digit sums, the Collatz conjecture and estimation (summary of NCERT Ganita Prakash Class 6)
meta_desc: Class 6 Number Play worksheet (Ganita Prakash Chapter 3): supercells, palindromes, the Kaprekar routine, digit sums, Collatz sequences and estimating. 100 questions with answers.
key_big: Numbers hide patterns: 6174 always appears in the Kaprekar routine
key_sub: A palindrome reads the same forwards and backwards.
body_html:
How it works

A palindrome reads the same both ways, like 4,334. Reversing a number and adding often leads to a palindrome: 57 + 75 = 132, 132 + 231 = 363.

Kaprekar routine: take a 4-digit number, arrange its digits from largest to smallest and smallest to largest, and subtract. Repeat — you always reach 6174.

Collatz: halve even numbers, and do 3 × n + 1 for odd numbers. Every starting number tried so far reaches 1.

Example

Kaprekar step for 3,524.

5,432 − 2,345

Answer: 3,087

Example

Collatz sequence from 6.

6 → 3 → 10 → 5 → 16 → 8 → 4 → 2 → 1

Answer: It reaches 1

Common mistakes

  • Subtracting the larger arrangement from the smaller.
  • Forgetting to reverse every digit when making a palindrome.
  • Halving an odd number in the Collatz rule instead of doing 3n + 1.

faq.a: 6174. Arranging the digits of a 4-digit number in descending and ascending order and subtracting, again and again, always reaches 6174 (if not all digits are the same).
A number that reads the same forwards and backwards, such as 121 or 4,554.
The guess that the rule 'halve if even, 3n + 1 if odd' always reaches 1, whatever number you start with.
